cards.title: Jobs Theory: Innovation Built on Causality, Not Correlation
cards.summary: Christensen's core argument that customers 'hire' products to make progress in a specific circumstance, and that this causal job — not demographics or product attributes — predicts innovation success.
cards.use_when: Framing an innovation or product strategy, or when your team's data is descriptive (who buys, what they look like) but cannot predict which new offer will succeed.
steps: Reframe the innovation question from 'how do we make our product better, more profitable, or more differentiated?' to 'what job did the customer hire this product to do?' (Christensen's central question).
Treat buying as hiring and quitting as firing: when a product does the job, it gets re-hired in the same circumstance; when it does the job badly, the customer fires it and looks for a replacement.

Accept that customer attributes (age, ZIP code, income, shoe size — Christensen's own example is that his height, age and shoe size never caused him to buy the New York Times) are not causal. Correlations can help describe a market but cannot reveal why a purchase happened.

Look for the circumstance, not the customer: a job arises from a situation ('long boring commute', 'want to say yes to my kid once this week'), and the same person can hire the same product for entirely different jobs at different times of day.

Use the job to redefine the competitive set. If margarine is hired to moisten bread so it's easier to chew, its competitors may be cream cheese, olive oil and mayonnaise; if hired to keep food from burning in a pan, competitors are Teflon and cooking spray in a different aisle.
Recognize that a market defined by internal category language ('yellow fats', 'spreads') is not how customers shop — they arrive with a specific job.
Expect the payoff to be predictability, not just post-hoc storytelling: the value of the theory is in predicting new successes, not celebrating past ones.
caveats: Jobs Theory tells you why customers make choices and what to build; it does not tell you whether a job is ethical to serve (Christensen notes cigarettes can be hired to satisfy jobs but harm the customer — ethical judgment is separate).
A job is a highly specific construct, not a catchphrase for something a customer wants or needs; the loose use of 'jobs' as a buzzword defeats the purpose.
Christensen claims the odds of creating exactly the right product even when a firm intends to disrupt are probably less than 25% 'if that' — presented as his estimate, not a measured benchmark.
Identifying the job is only the beginning; you still need to design the accompanying experiences and integrate internal capabilities, or the insight does not convert to advantage.

cards.title: The Milk Shake Study: Circumstance Interviews Beat Attribute Surveys
cards.summary: How a fast-food chain discovered two different jobs for the same milk shake by observing buyers and probing what else they hired instead, and why asking customers to improve the product produced zero sales change.
cards.use_when: Designing customer research for a product with flat or declining sales, or when survey feedback ('cheaper, chunkier, chewier') is producing changes that don't move the number.
steps: Run the conventional effort first if you must, to see its limits: the chain surveyed target-profile customers with 'How can we improve our milk shakes so you'd buy more? Do you want it cheaper? Chunkier? Chewier? Chocolatier?' and acted on the answers. Within months, sales of the category were unchanged.

Then observe instead of asking. The team stood in a restaurant for eighteen hours watching: what time people bought, what they wore, whether they were alone, whether they bought other food, and whether they stayed or drove off.
Note the pattern that emerged: a surprising share of shakes sold before 9 a.m. to solo customers who bought nothing else and left with it in the car.

Interview those buyers about the job, opening with an admission that you are puzzled ('What job were you trying to do that caused you to come here and hire that milk shake?'). Customers often cannot answer directly, so probe on what else they sometimes hired instead.

Collect the substitute set and each substitute's failure mode: bananas 'gone too quickly', doughnuts too crumbly and sticky on fingers and steering wheel, bagels dry and requiring two hands to spread, a Snickers bar that created guilt about candy for breakfast.

Identify the winning job statement in the customer's own terms: help me stay awake and occupied and make the morning commute more fun, while heading off mid-morning hunger. The thick shake through a thin straw took ~20 minutes and fit the cup holder.

Serve each job with its own design: for the commute job, a thicker shake (fruit or chocolate bits as surprise, for interest, not health) plus faster self-serve dispensing at the front counter with a swipe card; for the afternoon parent job, half sizes that finish quickly and reduce dad's guilt.
Note that the same product was competing against different things in each job — morning against bagels, bars and juice; afternoon against stopping at the toy store or a later game of catch.
Do not average the two jobs into one product. Christensen's explicit warning: averaging dad and commuter responses yields a one-size-fits-none shake that does neither job well.
caveats: This is a case study of one chain's discovery, not a promised sales outcome.
Demographics did not separate the morning buyers — what they shared was a job, not a profile.
The afternoon job is inferred from Christensen's own experience as a father in line; it illustrates the reasoning rather than reporting measured sales.

cards.title: Jobs Interviews: Track the Timeline of Triggers, Not Product Attributes
cards.summary: The interview method for surfacing a job: reconstruct the causal timeline of what happened before a purchase and avoid questions about the product's features.
cards.use_when: Building avatars, running win/loss or purchase interviews, or briefing an agency or researcher before qualitative fieldwork.
steps: Reconstruct the timeline of events and thoughts that led to the decision, in order, rather than asking for opinions about the product.
Do not focus on product attributes; the goal is the causal story of the choice, not feature preferences.
If the customer struggles to answer directly, ask what else they considered or sometimes hired instead of this product — substitutes expose the real competition and the real job.

Capture the language in the customer's own words, since the job statement should reflect their framing ('I'm full all morning', 'it fits right here in my cup holder') rather than the company's category vocabulary.
Treat the interview output as evidence: each avatar should carry quoted evidence plus the trigger moment and a job statement.
caveats: Attribute-focused interviews and direct feature requests are the failure mode this method is designed to replace — they tell you what people say they want, not why they chose.
A trigger moment and a job statement are presented as the minimum baseline for any avatar; how many avatars you end up with is not fixed by the method.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Push, Pull, Anxiety and Habit: The Forces Behind a Purchase Decision
cards.summary: A decision to change happens when the push of frustration plus the pull of the new solution outweighs the anxiety about the new and the habit of the present — useful as the diagnostic frame for avatar research.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why prospects stall mid-funnel, or structuring interview notes and avatar definitions around what actually triggered and blocked a switch.
steps: Map the push: the magnitude of the frustration in the current situation that makes the customer want to change at all.
Map the pull: the attraction of the new solution relative to the alternatives available for the same job.
Map the anxiety: the fears and uncertainties about adopting the new solution.
Map the habit: the inertia of the present behaviour that must be overcome for the switch to happen.
Treat the job spec as the output of this analysis: the tradeoffs the customer is willing to make, the competing solutions that must be beaten, and the obstacles that must be removed.
Use the balance to explain timing — a job sitting under strong habit and anxiety will not convert, however good the pull.
caveats: The four forces are a diagnostic frame for the decision, not a scoring model with published weights.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: What to Skip: Demographic Personas and Feature-Wish Surveys
cards.summary: Christensen's explicit list of research artefacts the jobs method rejects, and what to do instead.
cards.use_when: Auditing an existing avatar or persona deck, or approving a research brief, to check it is built on causal evidence rather than demographics.
steps: Skip persona templates that carry demographic fields and no job — anything that produces a fictional character with a stock photo.
Skip segmentation based on age, gender or income when it does not define the underlying causal mechanism.
Skip focus group data or surveys that simply ask customers what features they want added, without understanding the context of the job.
Avoid the Fallacy of Active Data: do not prioritise operations-related data (sales, customer characteristics) over the passive data of customer struggle.
Replace all of the above with the baseline: every avatar must contain quoted evidence, a trigger moment and a job statement.
Keep demographic facts only as context on the person, never as the explanatory mechanism for the choice.
caveats: The method is presented as universal, so the minimum requirements (evidence, trigger, job statement) apply to any avatar set; the number of avatars is explicitly not universal.
Christensen's own illustration: his age, height, shoe size and suburb did not cause him to buy the New York Times. Attributes can correlate with purchase propensity without causing it.
Correlation-based data is comfortable and makes managers sleep at night, which is why the fallacy is hard to shake — knowing it is a fallacy is not the same as acting on the difference.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Why Big Data and Customer Satisfaction Metrics Miss the Point
cards.summary: Data that groups customers by similarity or reports satisfaction cannot explain why a purchase happened, and assuming it can leads to churning out mediocrity.
cards.use_when: When a dashboard of demographics, market share and CSAT is being used as the basis for a product or growth decision.
steps: Recognise the shape of the data most companies hold: 'this customer looks like that one', 'this product has similar attributes to that one', 'these people behaved the same way in the past', or a preference split like '68% of customers say they prefer version A over version B'. None of it states why the choice was made.

Keep the correlation-versus-causation distinction operational, not decorative. Christensen cites Nate Silver: ice cream sales and forest fires correlate because both rise in summer heat, but buying a pint of Häagen-Dazs does not set the Montana brush on fire.

Watch for processes that operationalise a belief in randomness: if you believe innovation is unknowable and messy, you design a process that perfectly delivers messy, unknowable results. As Deming put it, every process is perfectly designed to deliver the results it gets.
Treat customer satisfaction metrics with suspicion for innovation purposes: they tell you whether a customer is happy, not how to do the job better — yet they are how most companies track success.
Ask better questions instead. Deming: if you do not know how to ask the right question, you discover nothing.

Beware stage-gates, six-sigma-style precision and rapid iteration applied to the wrong question: all that activity can give the illusion of progress without causing it, with R&D spend rising while breakthrough innovation is missed.
caveats: Christensen's framing of the data problem is an argument about explanatory power for innovation, not a claim that operations data has no value for running the business.
The 'less than 25%' odds figure is his estimate for hitting the right product, not a documented statistic from the sources cited.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Avoid Innovating Toward 'Average': The Jagged-Profile Lesson
cards.summary: The US Air Force cockpit case, retold by Christensen, shows that a design fitted to the average user fits nobody — a direct argument against averaging segment needs into one solution.
cards.use_when: When a roadmap item or landing page is being designed to 'work for everyone', or when multiple jobs are being averaged into a single offer.
steps: Recall the sequence: the Air Force assumed pilot control problems were training or pilot error, then found a cockpit designed around the 1920s average pilot.

They measured over four thousand pilots on nearly a dozen dimensions of size to update the average — then found that none of the pilots actually fell within the definition of average; every pilot had a jagged profile (some long legs, others long arms, height not corresponding to chest or head size).
The revised cockpits designed for everyone fit no one; the fix came only when baseline assumptions were swept aside and the adjustable seat was invented.

Apply the same logic to a jobs analysis: if morning commuters need a thick, slow shake and afternoon parents need a small, quickly finished one, do not design the average shake — design for each job or pick one deliberately.
In practice this argues for adjustability or genuinely distinct variants rather than one compromise offer.
caveats: This is an analogy from military procurement borrowed from Todd Rose's The End of Average; it is illustrative, not an ecommerce experiment.
It does not follow that every product must be customised — the lesson is against averaging incompatible jobs, not against standardisation.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Rewrite the Competitive Set as a Résumé of Alternatives
cards.summary: For any job, list every product the customer might hire and what each is good at, including items in entirely different aisles or categories, to see the real market size.
cards.use_when: Doing competitive analysis, sizing an opportunity, or repositioning a product that looks like a commodity inside its own category.
steps: State the job precisely first, because the competitor set changes with it. 'Moisten the crust on my bread so it's easier to chew' brings in butter, cream cheese, olive oil and mayonnaise. 'Keep my food from burning while cooking' brings in Teflon and nonstick spray, none of which sit in the cold foods aisle.
Write a résumé for each competing product: what job it gets hired for, in what circumstance, and where it falls short.
Accept that the same product can be hired for different jobs at different points in a customer's life, so one product may appear on several résumés.
Use the resumé lens to expose growth you cannot see through market share: Unilever held about 70% of US margarine, but no customer walks in asking for 'something in the yellow fats category'.

Check whether your differentiation is competing on an attribute irrelevant to the job — the twenty-one margarine SKUs differentiated on fat percentage, an attribute that did not map to any job Christensen and his daughter could observe.
Treat the competitive set as the design brief: the product must beat every alternative on the specific job, or the customer keeps hiring the substitute.
caveats: Christensen admits he and his daughter may not have identified all the substitutes correctly that day — the exercise is directional.

The Unilever episode is a negative case: the executives present were not moved by the reframe and the firm continued differentiating in traditional ways, with margarine later declining in US households amid trans-fat health concerns. The outcome is presented as an outsider's observation about a counterfactual, not proof that this lens would have saved the business.
Jobs Theory clarifies why customers choose, not whether the solution is good for them — trans-fat and ethical questions sit outside the theory.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: From Broken Category Assumptions to Growth: Disruption vs Jobs
cards.summary: Disruption explains how incumbents respond to threats but does not say where to look for growth; Jobs Theory is offered as the offensive complement.
cards.use_when: Choosing the strategic frame for an innovation programme, or when a disruption lens has identified a threat but produced no product roadmap.
steps: Use disruption for what it does: it explains and predicts incumbent behaviour in the face of a threat and helps incumbents judge which innovations on the horizon are the greatest disruptive threats.

Do not use disruption as an opportunity map. Christensen is explicit that it does not tell you where to look, how to undermine established leaders, where to create new markets, or which new products will succeed.
Be careful with the term itself: over two decades it has been stretched to mean anything clever, new and ambitious, which drains it of predictive power.
Use Jobs Theory for the offensive question — what causes customers to pull a product into their lives — since that is the causal mechanism behind successful innovation.

Apply this to ecommerce positioning: leaders often come close to the right idea and miss — AT&T showed a picture phone decades before the iPhone, major yogurt makers understood demand for Greek yogurt before Chobani's founder built a ~$1bn business. Knowing the demand exists is not the same as resolving the job, or the incumbent's constraints.
Expect different competitors, different priorities and different results once you adopt the jobs lens.
caveats: Christensen's claim that a well-defined job was implicitly at the core of most historic innovation successes is his belief, and he warns against relying on retrospective explanation — the value is in prediction.
This is theory framing from a 2016 book; treat the named company trajectories as examples at a point in time.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Why Smart Managers Fail: Processes Perfectly Designed for Mediocrity
cards.summary: Great managers following all the best advice can still lead firms to the top and off a cliff, and the 'stupid manager' explanation collapses when a whole industry falls at once.
cards.use_when: Post-mortems where leadership failure is the assumed explanation, or when building an innovation process that you expect to produce breakthroughs.
steps: Distrust the management-quality narrative. Digital Equipment Corporation's success was attributed to the brilliance of its management and its collapse to the ineptitude of the same people — Christensen asks how smart people get so stupid so fast.
Test the individual-blame hypothesis against the industry: almost every minicomputer company in the world collapsed in unison, which points to something structural rather than a few bad leaders.

Accept that disciplined processes can be the problem. Careful stage-gates, rapid iteration, checks and balances, calculated risks and six-sigma-derived requirements give the appearance of a mastered scientific process while innovation stays hit or miss.

Notice the evidence of wasted effort: 84% of global executives in a McKinsey poll said innovation was extremely important, 94% were unsatisfied with their own innovation performance, and one thousand publicly held companies spent $680bn on R&D in 2015, up 5.1% — more activity and more data without more breakthroughs.
Diagnose your own process for whether it is designed around a belief that innovation is random; if so, it will keep delivering randomness even with better talent and bigger budgets.
caveats: The poll, spend and satisfaction figures are cited from period sources (McKinsey; strategy+business, 2015) and describe that period, not current benchmarks.
The DEC 'stupid manager' critique is an argument about structural causes, not a denial that management matters.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Recognising a Job: Little and Big, Predictable and Sudden
cards.summary: Jobs arise from situations; classifying them by size and predictability helps a team notice which jobs its product could plausibly be hired for.
cards.use_when: Generating job hypotheses in a workshop before doing timeline interviews, or mapping where an offer might fit into a customer's day.
steps: Start from the premise that every day things happen to us and jobs arise that need to be done; when a job arises, the customer reaches out and pulls something into their life to get it done.
Sort candidates by scale: little jobs such as 'pass the time while waiting in line', big jobs such as 'find a more fulfilling career'.

Sort by predictability: some jobs surface unpredictably, like dressing for an out-of-town meeting after the airline loses your suitcase; others are regular, like packing a healthy, tasty lunch for a daughter to take to school.

Use the classification to see how the same product can be pulled in for different reasons — the New York Times might be hired to fill waiting-room time, to serve March Madness basketball interest, or to be delivered to the door so neighbours see you as informed.
Note that no ZIP code or median household income figure would reveal the last of those reasons, which is why circumstance beats demographic inference.
caveats: These are illustrative examples from the book, not a taxonomy with operational thresholds.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: It's Not Just About Jobs: Experiences and Integration Create the Moat
cards.summary: Identifying the job is only the start; competitors can copy products but not well-integrated experiences, which is where sustained advantage sits.
cards.use_when: Planning what happens after a jobs insight is validated — turning it into a blueprint, an experience and internal process change.
steps: Translate the job insight into a blueprint that guides development of the product or service and, crucially, the set of experiences that accompany it in solving the job.
Then integrate the company's internal capabilities and processes so the job is nailed consistently, rather than solved well once.
Treat integration as the defensible part: Christensen notes it may be easy for competitors to copy products but difficult to copy experiences integrated into your processes.
Expect the effort to be holistic — from the original insight through to the product reaching the consumer, involving decisions and influence from virtually everyone in the company.

Protect against internal drift: return on net assets pressures, well-intentioned efficiency drives and everyday frontline decisions can quietly break the delivery of a solution you already understood correctly.
Note the payoff asymmetry: even innovators clear about the jobs their products are hired for can lose their way, so the theory is not self-executing.
caveats: Presented as the authors' framework across chapters 6 to 8; the specifics of implementation are not detailed in this section.
Christensen's claim that experiences are harder to copy than products is a strategic argument, not an experimental result.
